title: Nope
author: Debra Ducane
cast: Michael Busch as Jean Jacket (the creature)

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Nope is not a woke trap — it's an honest genre film with a Black filmmaker's thematic preoccupations baked visibly into its DNA. The film's central argument about spectacle and exploitation is made through horror mechanics rather than political lecture, and the Black family at its center is defined by work ethic, craft, and legacy rather than victimhood. Conservative audiences may not love every element but they won't feel ambushed.

director.name: Jordan Peele
director.ideology: Progressive/Afrocentric
director.profile:
Jordan Peele is one of contemporary Hollywood's most interesting filmmakers and one of its most politically self-conscious. Get Out (2017) announced him as a filmmaker with an original and specific voice — a horror auteur using genre mechanics to process Black American anxieties about white liberal spaces. Us (2019) was more ambitious and more obscure, and Nope is the most formally confident and narratively opaque film of the three.

Peele's politics are progressive and his films are marked by them — he is interested in racial history, in the mechanics of exploitation, in who gets to tell stories and who gets erased from them. But he is also a genuine craftsman who understands that ideology delivered as lecture kills genre. His best instincts are as a filmmaker first. Nope shows him at his most technically ambitious — the cinematography (Hoyte van Hoytema, the DP for Dunkirk and Interstellar) is extraordinary — and at his most thematically restrained. The film's argument about spectacle emerges from what you watch, not from what characters say.

writer.name: Jordan Peele
writer.profile: Peele's screenplay is his most structurally unusual. Nope operates on two parallel tracks — the UFO horror plot and the Gordy's Home chimpanzee massacre subplot — that are thematically connected but causally independent. The screenplay trusts the audience to hold both tracks in mind and make the thematic connection without being walked through it. This is ambitious writing, and it mostly works. The Gordy flashback sequences are the film's most formally daring material.

top_cast: Daniel Kaluuya as OJ Haywood — Kaluuya is doing something technically extraordinary here: he's playing a man who expresses almost nothing verbally and communicates almost everything physically. OJ Haywood is a stoic — a man defined by craft, by responsibility to his family's legacy, by the quiet dignity of doing difficult work well. In a cinematic landscape where Black male characters are expected to be expressive and emotionally available, Kaluuya's choice to play OJ as a Western-genre archetype (the laconic ranch hand who turns out to be the most capable man in any room) is both a directorial and a personal statement.

Keke Palmer as Emerald Haywood — Palmer provides the film's kinetic energy, and she earns every scene she's given. Emerald is the extrovert to OJ's introvert — entrepreneurial, reckless, genuinely funny — and Palmer plays the character's hunger for spectacle with enough self-awareness to make her eventual reckoning hit. The sibling dynamic between Kaluuya and Palmer is the film's warmest element.

Steven Yeun as Ricky 'Jupe' Park — the film's most disturbing performance, and deliberately understated. Jupe is a former child star who survived a traumatic on-set incident and has since built an entire personality around his ability to metabolize horror into entertainment. Yeun plays him as permanently slightly off — enthusiastic in a way that reads as disassociation — and the character is the film's clearest statement about what spectacle does to the people inside it.
top_performers: Daniel Kaluuya as OJ Haywood — the year's best performance in a major studio film, all restraint and physical authority
Steven Yeun as Ricky Park — plays trauma-as-showmanship with uncomfortable precision
bottom_performers: Brandon Perea as Angel Torres — reliable comic relief but the character is functional rather than memorable

fidelity_casting.summary: Nope is an original story with no source material casting constraints, built around a Black family who owns a horse ranch in the Agua Dulce area of California. The Haywood family's identity — their claim to be the descendants of the first person ever filmed, a Black jockey in Eadweard Muybridge's 1887 motion studies — is thematically central and historically grounded. The casting is purpose-built and the choices are uniformly strong.

content_warnings: Graphic violence including a chimpanzee attack with disturbing injuries shown
Characters consumed by a creature with visceral on-screen effect
Sustained horror atmosphere with intense sequences throughout
Brief profanity and crude language
Themes of trauma, death, and exploitation
family_discussion_topics: What does it mean to 'get the shot' — when does capturing something become exploiting it?
The film opens with a Biblical verse about spectacle and judgment. What do you think Peele is saying?
parental_guidance.recommendation: This is a hard R and earns it. The Gordy chimpanzee attack sequence is genuinely disturbing — not gratuitous, but the violence is specific and the aftermath is shown. Not appropriate for anyone under 17. Strong recommendation for mature teens and adults who like serious, formally ambitious genre filmmaking.

summary.overall:
Jordan Peele's third film is his most formally ambitious and his most politically restrained, which may be why it polarized audiences in ways his earlier work didn't. Get Out operated as a precise political metaphor — white liberals harvesting Black bodies — and the clarity of that metaphor was part of its pleasure. Nope refuses that clarity. It has a thesis about spectacle and exploitation, but the thesis lives in the film's structure and imagery rather than in its dialogue. This is more interesting and less satisfying, which is exactly the trade-off serious filmmaking tends to make.

The Haywood family runs a horse ranch in Agua Dulce, California. Their father's business is supplying horses to Hollywood productions — an honest, skilled, unglamorous trade. When something in the sky starts eating their horses, the film becomes a UFO thriller that is also, somehow, a meditation on who gets credit for images and who gets consumed by them. The film opens with a cryptic Biblical epigraph from Nahum: 'I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a spectacle.' Peele is not making a subtle film. He is making a film whose subtlety lives in how it earns its thesis rather than in whether it has one.

The decision to cast Daniel Kaluuya as OJ Haywood is the most consequential creative choice in the film, and it earns its own paragraph. OJ is a stoic — a man who communicates through the physical language of horse training, through the competence and patience his work requires, through a quietness that reads as depth rather than blankness. Kaluuya plays him as a Western-genre archetype: the laconic ranch hand who is the most capable person in any situation and needs no one to acknowledge it. In a Hollywood landscape that typically requires Black male leads to perform emotional accessibility, this is a pointed choice. OJ Haywood is not here to explain himself to you. He's here to do the work.

The Gordy subplot — in which a former child star named Jupe Park (Steven Yeun) witnessed the on-set massacre perpetrated by a trained chimpanzee named Gordy — is the film's most formally daring gambit and its most disturbing passage. Peele cuts between the present-day UFO plot and the Gordy incident in a way that establishes the film's thematic argument without stating it: both plots are about the cost of trying to domesticate something wild and spectacular for human entertainment. The chimpanzee was trained to perform. The creature in the sky is being trained to perform. The people who built their personalities around proximity to the spectacle are the ones who get consumed. This is not a subtle reading, but it's an earned one.

Nope's final sequence — OJ on horseback, attempting to hold the creature's attention long enough for Emerald to photograph it, Holst ascending with his IMAX camera to be devoured — is the film's thesis made visual. What we see, and whether seeing it dignifies or exploits what is seen, is the film's real subject. Peele doesn't resolve this tension; he frames it, which is the more honest choice. For a filmmaker whose first two films offered the reassurance of clear villains and clear victims, Nope is a genuine evolution. It will reward the viewer who brings patience and frustrate the one who came for another Get Out.
summary.verdict_explanation: Nope earns MIXED BAG because it's genuinely excellent filmmaking (extraordinary cinematography, career-best Kaluuya performance, formally ambitious structure) in service of thematic material that contains both traditional elements (family legacy, work ethic, stoic masculine competence) and progressive ones (spectacle-as-exploitation, historical erasure of Black labor). The traditional elements outweigh the woke ones, but it's not a traditional film.
summary.adultInsight: Nope was Peele's biggest budget to date — Universal gave him $68 million, up significantly from Get Out's $4.5 million — and the film's use of that budget is instructive. Rather than scale up the horror-thriller formula that made him bankable, Peele spent the money on IMAX cameras, practical effects, and a DP (Hoyte van Hoytema) associated with Christopher Nolan's most technically ambitious work. The result looks unlike any other major studio horror film of its era. Peele is clearly using his cultural capital to make the kind of formally serious genre cinema that studios rarely fund — and the film's mixed commercial reception ($171M on a $68M budget is profitable but not the hit Get Out was) may explain why the fourth Peele film has been slow to materialize.

tropeAudit.name: Stoic Masculine Competence
tropeAudit.analysis: OJ Haywood is a classically stoic protagonist — a man who communicates through action and craft rather than self-expression, who earns authority through demonstrated competence rather than status, and whose emotional depth is visible only to the audience, never performed for other characters. This archetype is as old as the Western genre and Peele deploys it with full consciousness of its history.

tropeAudit.name: Family Legacy and Craft
tropeAudit.analysis: The Haywood family's identity is defined by their work — they train horses, they have always trained horses, and this continuity of craft across generations is presented as dignity-giving rather than limiting. The film opens by establishing that a Haywood ancestor was the first person ever filmed, and the family's mission to finally get credit for that is the narrative engine. This is conservative in the best sense: honoring the specific, tangible labor of those who came before.

tropeAudit.name: Spectacle as Exploitation — Anti-Consumption Thesis
tropeAudit.analysis: The film's central argument — that spectacle consumes what it depicts, that the camera extracts value from its subjects without their consent — maps onto progressive critiques of media, capitalism, and the entertainment industry's relationship to minority communities. The thesis is made through genre mechanics rather than dialogue, which is the most defensible way to make a political argument in horror film. But the argument is there.

tropeAudit.name: Historical Erasure of Black Labor
tropeAudit.analysis: The film's framing device — that a Black jockey was the first person ever captured on motion picture film but was denied credit, his face deliberately obscured in reproductions — is historically informed (the Muybridge horse studies are real) and politically conscious. Peele is making a point about whose contributions get acknowledged and whose get absorbed. The point is valid but the framing is consistent with progressive historical grievance narratives.

tropeAudit.name: Sacrifice for Others
tropeAudit.analysis: OJ's final act — riding into the creature's field of vision to hold its attention at the cost of his own life, giving Emerald time to complete their mission — is a traditional sacrificial heroism arc executed without irony or subversion. The film earns this beat because OJ's entire characterization has been in service of it: he is a man who puts the work and the people he loves above his own safety, and the film honors this without eulogizing it.

tropeAudit.name: Sibling Bond as Emotional Core
tropeAudit.analysis: The relationship between OJ and Emerald Haywood is the film's warmest element and its most traditional structure. Their dynamic — the quiet, responsible older sibling and the charismatic, reckless younger one — is a family archetype as old as storytelling, and Kaluuya and Palmer play it with genuine tenderness. The film's emotional stakes are entirely about this relationship, not about ideology.

comparison_films.title: Get Out (2017)
comparison_films.comparison: Peele's debut is tighter, cleaner, and more politically precise. Get Out works as both a horror film and a political metaphor because the metaphor is clear and the horror mechanics serve it without friction. Nope is more formally ambitious and thematically richer but less satisfying as a unified experience. As a filmmaker, Peele is growing in ways that his audience may not always follow.

comparison_films.title: Signs (2002)
comparison_films.comparison: M. Night Shyamalan's UFO thriller is the most obvious genre comparison, and Peele is clearly aware of it. Both films use alien threat as a lens for family dynamics and larger questions about faith and meaning. Signs resolves its ambiguities theologically; Nope refuses resolution. Signs is the more comforting film; Nope is the more honest one.

comparison_films.title: Jaws (1975)
comparison_films.comparison: The original blueprint for the monster-as-force-of-nature thriller informs Nope at every level — the choice to keep the creature off-screen for most of the film, the ensemble structure, the climactic confrontation that requires the protagonists to use the monster's nature against it. Peele is working consciously in Spielberg's tradition while using it to make arguments Spielberg wouldn't.

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Don't Worry Darling qualifies as a woke trap. It was marketed and sold as a sexy, stylish psychological thriller with gorgeous 1950s production design, Florence Pugh, and Harry Styles. Trailers emphasized lush visuals, marital passion, and a mysterious cult-like community. Olivia Wilde promoted it as a film about female pleasure and female gaze in cinema. What audiences got instead was an anti-patriarchy polemic with a specific ideological target that director Wilde revealed only in post-release interviews: the villain Frank is explicitly based on Jordan Peterson, whom Wilde publicly described as a hero to the incel community. This framing was never in the marketing. The simulation premise (that Jack drugged Alice and put her in a coma against her will to trap her in a 1950s VR world where women serve men) is not revealed until roughly the 80-minute mark in a 123-minute film. The film's true ideological argument, that traditional domesticity itself is a prison men construct to control women, is smuggled inside a thriller structure. Conservative families drawn in by the period aesthetics and star power will not discover the full ideological payload until well past the halfway point.

director.name: Olivia Wilde
director.ideology: Progressive feminist. Wilde is an outspoken liberal activist whose public statements consistently reflect progressive ideology on gender, sexuality, and politics.
director.profile: Olivia Wilde is an actress turned director whose feature debut Booksmart (2019) earned strong critical praise as a female-led coming-of-age comedy with a progressive bent. Don't Worry Darling was her follow-up, and she approached it with explicit ideological intent. In a widely reported interview with Maggie Gyllenhaal, Wilde stated that the villain Frank was based on Jordan Peterson, calling him a 'pseudo-intellectual hero to the incel community.' She described the film as being about women reclaiming agency from men who need to control them. The production was marked by reported conflicts between Wilde and lead actress Florence Pugh, the high-profile circumstances of Shia LaBeouf's replacement by Harry Styles, and tabloid coverage that dominated the film's Venice Film Festival rollout.

writer.name: Katie Silberman
writer.profile: Katie Silberman co-wrote Booksmart with Wilde and returned for Don't Worry Darling. She adapted the original spec script by brothers Carey Van Dyke and Shane Van Dyke, substantially reworking it to incorporate the feminist ideological framework Wilde wanted. The original spec reportedly did not include the anti-incel Jordan Peterson angle. That was Wilde and Silberman's addition. Silberman also co-wrote Set It Up (2018) for Netflix.

top_cast.name: Florence Pugh
top_cast.notes: Pugh is the best thing in this film by a significant margin. Her performance as Alice, moving from contented housewife to increasingly destabilized woman to terrified prisoner to furious survivor, is genuinely compelling. Whatever behind-the-scenes tension existed between Pugh and Wilde, it did not diminish Pugh's commitment to the role. Pugh has been public about her concern that the film's marketing oversold the 'female empowerment' angle at the expense of the thriller mechanics. She is correct. She delivers a performance that deserves a sharper screenplay.

top_cast.name: Harry Styles
top_cast.notes: Styles is the film's weak link. As the charming husband who is actually holding his wife captive in a simulated reality against her will, Styles lacks the menace the role requires. His performance is likable when the character needs to be frightening, and soft when it needs to be threatening. The casting of a pop star beloved by a younger female demographic, which Wilde leaned into heavily in marketing, undercuts the film's own thesis about dangerous men.

top_cast.name: Chris Pine
top_cast.notes: Pine is the film's most effective performer in the villain role. His Frank is controlled, charismatic, and genuinely unsettling. The dinner scene where he calmly dares Alice to challenge him while making her look delusional is the film's best sequence. Pine reportedly was not informed by Wilde that Frank was based on Jordan Peterson until late in production.

top_cast.name: Olivia Wilde
top_cast.notes: Wilde cast herself as Alice's best friend, who turns out to have known the simulation's true nature all along. The twist that Bunny chose to stay in the simulation because her real children died is the film's most emotionally honest moment. It is also the scene Wilde plays best.

The ideological content frames traditional gender roles and the stay-at-home wife dynamic as inherently sinister and dehumanizing. This is not a film for families or for viewers who will find its ideological framing offensive. Adults who want a stylish psychological thriller with capable craft and will engage critically with its politics can find value in Florence Pugh's performance and the production design. Everyone else should know exactly what they're getting.

summary.overall:
Don't Worry Darling is a film with a beautiful surface and a sermon underneath. Olivia Wilde's second feature arrives packaged as a sexy, sun-drenched psychological thriller with Florence Pugh, Harry Styles, and some of the most luscious 1950s production design seen on a major studio film. What it actually is is a feminist polemic with a specific target that Wilde identified only after the cameras stopped rolling: the villain is Jordan Peterson.

That revelation, delivered in a Maggie Gyllenhaal interview, clarified what the film's structure had made somewhat murky. Victory, California, the idyllic desert company town where husbands go to mysterious work and wives tend perfect homes, is not a generic authoritarian dystopia. It is a specifically anti-incel, anti-manosphere fantasy. The men running Victory have built a virtual reality prison for women who refused to be wives, then uploaded them without consent. The pitch is made explicit in Wilde's public commentary: incels are 'disenfranchised, mostly white men' who want the 1950s back, and this is the horror that results.

Here is the problem with Don't Worry Darling as cinema, separate from its ideology: it does not earn its thesis. Wilde and writer Katie Silberman adapted an original spec script by the Van Dyke brothers and substantially rewrote it to carry this ideological payload. The resulting film is visually assured, occasionally genuinely suspenseful, and built around a Florence Pugh performance that is too good for the movie it's in. It is also paced badly, logically inconsistent (the mechanics of the simulation never withstand scrutiny), and derailed by the well-publicized behind-the-scenes drama that made the film's Venice premiere more interesting as tabloid fodder than as cinema.

Plot Summary: Paradise Is a Prison

Alice and Jack Chambers live in Victory, California, an impossibly perfect desert community in the late 1950s or early 1960s. The aesthetic is impeccable: pool parties, Cadillacs, cocktails at sundown, wives in full skirts waving goodbye as husbands leave for the Victory Project headquarters in the surrounding hills. The men work on 'progressive materials,' a vague description that satisfies no one who asks. Wives are expected not to visit headquarters. The community patriarch, Frank, radiates charismatic authority at regular social events. Alice is happy, or appears to be.

The cracks begin when Alice witnesses a neighbor, Margaret, become increasingly erratic. Margaret's young son apparently died in the desert near headquarters. She insists the company took him as punishment. She slits her own throat in front of Alice and falls from her roof. Victory tells Alice that Margaret simply had an accident.

Alice begins having visions: a life in the 21st century, residency as a surgeon, an unemployment check with Jack's name on it. The visions intensify. When she reaches the headquarters building and touches its mirrored surface, she experiences what feels like another life entirely.

The film's second half accelerates toward its reveal: Victory is a simulation. The men logged out each day to work and maintain their real-world access while their wives remained uploaded, unconscious in the real world, living out the perfect domesticity their husbands wanted for them. Jack, who was unemployed in reality while Alice worked brutal hospital shifts, found Victory and uploaded her against her will. He drugged her, strapped her down, and put her in a coma so she could keep his house. He tells her, with genuine belief in his own argument, that she was miserable in the real world. She was happy here. He did it for her.

Alice kills Jack. She drives to headquarters. The screen goes black.

A note on the woke scoring: we rate the authenticity of 'traditional domesticity as prison' as High because Wilde stated this explicitly in multiple interviews. This is not a reading critics projected onto the film; it is the director's stated intent. The Jordan Peterson villain coding is rated High for the same reason. When a director tells you what she made, you believe her.

The film's only genuine traditional score comes from Bunny's subplot. Her choice to stay in the simulation, knowing it is false, because her real children died and here she can be with them, is the film's most honest emotional beat. It is also, notably, the one place where the film presents a woman's domestic attachment to her children as something other than manufactured oppression. Wilde plays this scene herself.

Woke Trap Assessment

Don't Worry Darling is a woke trap. The film was marketed on aesthetics, star power, and the promise of a sexy thriller. Trailers showed 1950s glamour, suggestive imagery from what was promoted as an explicit female-gaze love scene, and Florence Pugh looking increasingly terrified. No trailer foregrounded the film's ideological argument. The Jordan Peterson villain angle was not disclosed until Wilde's Gyllenhaal interview after production.

The full simulation reveal comes at roughly the 80-minute mark of a 123-minute film. Before that point, the film operates as a genuine mystery thriller with feminist overtones that could plausibly be read as genre atmosphere rather than ideology. The specific political target becomes clear only in the final act, and was confirmed explicitly only by Wilde's post-release comments.

Conservative families attracted by the period setting and the Styles/Pugh star power will discover the film's actual content well past the halfway point.

Creative Team at a Glance

Olivia Wilde's ideological track record as a director is brief but consistent. Booksmart (2019) celebrated female friendship and progressive values within a coming-of-age comedy frame without announcing its politics loudly. Don't Worry Darling is the same approach scaled up and aimed at a more explicitly ideological target. The difference is that Booksmart was honest about what it was.

Katie Silberman's co-writing credits run progressive throughout. Set It Up was a light romantic comedy. Booksmart was a female buddy film. Don't Worry Darling represents her most overtly political work.

Wilde and Silberman's stated creative process on this film is instructive: they took a spec script that had no ideological content and rewrote it to carry a specific anti-incel, anti-manosphere argument while the studio sold it as a stylish thriller. That gap between product and marketing defines a woke trap.

Adult Viewer Insight

The behind-the-scenes drama surrounding Don't Worry Darling is more interesting than the film itself, and it undercuts the film's feminist thesis in an ironic way Wilde seems not to have noticed.

Florencia Pugh, who delivers the film's best performance and drives every scene she is in, was reportedly not happy with the marketing's emphasis on the Harry Styles sex scene and the 'female empowerment' framing over the actual thriller mechanics. This tension between a lead actress who wanted the film judged on craft and a director who wanted it judged on politics played out visibly at Venice, where Pugh gave a cold shoulder to Wilde on multiple occasions and delivered a diplomatic non-answer when asked about their working relationship.

The film's thesis is that men construct systems to keep women in service roles. The film was directed by a woman who reportedly had a difficult relationship with her female lead, reportedly promised a role to Shia LaBeouf and then disputed the circumstances of his departure, and promoted a film about female agency by centering male star power in every piece of marketing. Jordan Peterson as villain. Harry Styles's body in every trailer. The contradiction is not subtle.

For viewers who can engage with this material critically rather than as converts or opponents, Don't Worry Darling is a genuinely interesting case study in how ideological filmmaking can undermine itself when the execution does not match the ambition. Pugh's performance is worth watching. The simulation mechanics do not hold up to any scrutiny. The final image, Alice gasping as she escapes the simulation, is earned emotionally but leaves the film with no conclusion. What is Alice returning to? An unemployed husband she killed (in the real world). A life she hated. The film has no answer because it was only ever interested in the escape, not the landing.
summary.adultInsight: Don't Worry Darling is an ideologically transparent feminist thriller that was marketed as something more neutral and glossy than it is. Director Olivia Wilde confirmed in post-release interviews that villain Frank was explicitly modeled on Jordan Peterson as a proxy for incel/manosphere ideology. The film's central premise, men trapping women in a simulated 1950s domestic paradise without consent, is designed as a metaphor for patriarchal control of women's roles and bodies. The woke content is not ambiguous or subtle: traditional domesticity is literally a prison built by men to serve their needs. The film's production was marked by reported Wilde/Pugh tensions, disputed circumstances around LaBeouf's departure, and Venice tabloid chaos that dominated coverage. Florence Pugh's performance is the film's legitimate artistic achievement. Harry Styles's casting is the film's most visible commercial compromise. The simulation's internal logic does not survive scrutiny. Verdict: a stylish package delivering an explicit progressive ideological payload about patriarchal control dressed as a thriller twist.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R. Not appropriate for children or teens. Multiple explicit sex scenes, including one marketed extensively as 'female gaze' erotica. Non-consensual captivity and drug-induced imprisonment are the horror at the film's center. A character commits suicide on screen. The ideological content frames traditional gender roles and homemaking as dehumanizing male-constructed prisons. Conservative families should be aware this is precisely the opposite of a traditional values film despite its vintage aesthetic.

tropeAudit.name: Traditional Domesticity as Male-Constructed Prison
tropeAudit.description: The entire premise of Don't Worry Darling is that the 1950s domestic ideal, the stay-at-home wife keeping a perfect house while her husband does meaningful work, is not an organic arrangement or a legitimate choice. It is a prison men built specifically to trap women who would not otherwise submit. Frank's Victory Project physically simulates this arrangement. The women inside it cannot leave, cannot question, and were placed there without consent. The 1950s aesthetic is explicitly coded as what dangerous men want for women. Director Wilde confirmed this in interviews.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Patriarchy Feminist Manifesto
tropeAudit.description: The film's ideological thesis is not incidental or submerged. Wilde designed Don't Worry Darling as a feminist thriller explicitly about men's need to control women. Frank's community is a patriarchy made literal: men control the world, women serve in it, and any woman who questions this is labeled mentally ill and medicated. The parallels to contemporary feminist critiques of domestic expectations are intentional and confirmed by the filmmakers.

tropeAudit.name: Non-Consent / Bodily Autonomy as Central Horror
tropeAudit.description: The film's horror pivot depends entirely on the revelation that Alice is in the simulation not by choice but because Jack drugged her and placed her there against her will. Her body is literally imprisoned without consent. The film frames this as the logical endpoint of men who want domestic wives: when women won't comply willingly, they take compliance by force. This is not subtext. It is the explicit narrative argument.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Incel/Anti-Manosphere Ideological Coding
tropeAudit.description: Wilde stated in interviews that villain Frank was based on Jordan Peterson, whom she described as a pseudo-intellectual hero to the incel community. This was not in the film's marketing. Chris Pine's Frank runs a community for men who feel the world has failed them, promises a return to masculine purpose and female domestic compliance, and uses ideology to recruit followers. The parallel to online manosphere recruitment is intentional. Wilde also described incels as 'disenfranchised, mostly white men' in press materials.

tropeAudit.name: Male Authority as Abuse
tropeAudit.description: Every male authority figure in Don't Worry Darling is either an active oppressor (Frank, Jack) or a complicit enabler (Dr. Collins). No male character operates as a positive counterweight. The film's visual grammar consistently frames male authority in terms of surveillance and control: Frank watching Jack and Alice's intimate moment unbeknownst to them, the electroconvulsive therapy administered by the male physician, the men in red jumpsuits who drag Alice away from inconvenient truths.

tropeAudit.name: Female Resilience and Survival
tropeAudit.description: Alice's survival and escape is driven by raw determination and refusal to accept the reality she's been given. This quality, in a different film, would register as straightforward heroism. Here it is instrumentalized in service of the film's feminist thesis, which diminishes its authenticity as a standalone traditional value. Alice survives not through strength of character in the classical sense but through ideological awakening. Still, the survival instinct and physical courage she demonstrates are genuinely present.

tropeAudit.name: Maternal Love as Authentic Motivation
tropeAudit.description: Bunny's reveal that she chose to remain in the simulation because her children died in the real world and here she can be with them is the film's most genuinely moving moment. It presents maternal love as a force powerful enough to override freedom itself. This is an unambiguously traditional value embedded in the film, and it is given to the character Wilde plays herself. It is also the film's only concession that the domestic world of Victory contains something real and worth protecting.

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Babylon is not a woke trap. The film's hedonism, excess, drug use, sexual content, and moral chaos are visible from the opening sequence of the premiere party with its orgy, cocaine, and bodily fluids. Nothing is hidden. The progressive character elements (Lady Fay Zhu as an openly gay woman, Sidney Palmer's blackface subplot) are present throughout. The film does not masquerade as a traditional values piece. Its TRADITIONAL LEAN score comes from its honest portrayal of excess and destruction: every character who surrenders to the decadence of 1920s Hollywood loses everything. Damien Chazelle is making a film about the cost of living outside moral structure, and the wages-of-sin pattern runs through the entire narrative arc even if Chazelle would not use that language.

director.name: Damien Chazelle
director.ideology: Moderate/Liberal. Chazelle is an apolitical filmmaker by public profile. His ideology expresses through craft obsession and themes of ambition, excellence, and the price of artistic pursuit rather than social commentary.
director.profile: Damien Chazelle is the director of Whiplash (2014), La La Land (2016), First Man (2018), and Babylon (2022). He became the youngest Best Director winner in Oscar history at age 32 for La La Land. Chazelle's films consistently examine the cost of obsessive excellence and the people sacrificed on the altar of ambition. Babylon is his most unrestrained work: a 189-minute period epic that appears to celebrate Hollywood's first golden age while systematically dismantling every character who reaches too high. His influences include Scorsese, Altman, Fellini, and the French New Wave. He is not a political filmmaker in any conventional sense, and Babylon does not function as a politically motivated film. It functions as a moral epic dressed in debauchery.

writer.name: Damien Chazelle
writer.profile: Chazelle wrote and directed Babylon solo. The screenplay was developed over several years and represents his most ambitious structural undertaking: an ensemble portrait of five characters across a decade, built around the Hollywood transition from silent films to sound. His research drew on the documented history of the era, including the real scandals, casting practices, and industry machinery of 1920s-1930s Hollywood. Critics noted some historical liberties. The script's most debated element is its maximalist structure: at 189 minutes, it runs longer than the patience of many viewers who came expecting the elegance of La La Land.

composer.name: Justin Hurwitz
composer.profile: Justin Hurwitz has scored every Chazelle film. His Babylon score is genuinely extraordinary: a propulsive, jazz-drenched, anachronistic mix that drives the party sequences like a locomotive and then drops into melancholy for the film's quieter moments. The score won the Golden Globe for Best Original Score and received an Oscar nomination. It may be the film's single greatest artistic achievement and arguably the best film score of 2022.

top_cast.name: Margot Robbie
top_cast.notes: Robbie gives the performance of her career as Nellie LaRoy, the self-proclaimed star from New Jersey who burns her way through Hollywood like a lit fuse. Nellie is pure id: magnetic, reckless, hilarious, heartbreaking. She dominates every room she walks into and destroys every stable thing around her. Robbie commits completely, going from manic comedy to raw vulnerability in single shots. The scene where she fights a rattlesnake at a party, drunk and giggling, is both absurd and genuinely frightening. This is the role that should have made her an Oscar winner.

top_cast.name: Brad Pitt
top_cast.notes: Pitt plays a fading silent film star with the particular melancholy of a man who knows exactly what he is losing and cannot stop it. His Jack Conrad is generous, romantic, and fundamentally decent in a film full of selfish people. He marries and divorces multiple times. He is honest with himself when few others in the film are. His final scene, attending a screening of Singin' in the Rain alone and weeping because he has been immortalized in a culture that discarded him, is one of the most quietly devastating sequences in recent Hollywood filmmaking.

top_cast.name: Diego Calva
top_cast.notes: Calva is the film's moral center and its most underrated element. Manny is the witness through whom we observe Babylon's excess: a Mexican immigrant who climbs from elephant handler to studio executive through talent, work ethic, and love for cinema itself. His loyalty to Nellie LaRoy, long after she has given him every reason to walk away, is the film's most sustained traditional value. Calva's restraint against Robbie's explosion and Pitt's charisma is an act of disciplined craft that the film requires.

top_cast.name: Jean Smart
top_cast.notes: Smart plays the gossip columnist with the mordant wit the role demands. Her scene with Jack Conrad, telling him his star has faded but he will be immortalized, contains more honest emotion than most of Babylon's louder sequences. Smart has the film's wisest line: that cinema matters not because of what any individual makes, but because of what the medium preserves.

top_cast.name: Jovan Adepo
top_cast.notes: Adepo plays a jazz trumpeter whose talent and integrity collide with Hollywood's racism. The blackface sequence, where studio executives demand he darken his comparatively light skin to satisfy Southern audiences who object to interracial orchestras, is the film's most politically explicit moment and its most historically honest. Sidney's departure from Hollywood is handled with dignity rather than as a political lecture.

fidelity_casting.summary: Original screenplay. Characters are loosely inspired by real Hollywood figures of the era. Jack Conrad draws from several silent era stars. Nellie LaRoy is a composite of era starlets. No direct adaptations requiring fidelity assessment.

parental_guidance.recommendation: Not appropriate for anyone under 18. Babylon earns its R rating repeatedly and enthusiastically. The opening party sequence is one of the most graphically debaucherous in mainstream studio filmmaking in years: explicit sex acts, cocaine being consumed openly, nudity, and a scene involving an elephant that cannot be described here. The film maintains this intensity intermittently for its entire 189 minutes. This is not a film for families. Conservative viewers who want to see a serious cinematic statement about the cost of excess and the enduring power of art will find it in Babylon, but they will earn that finding the hard way. Consider yourself warned.

summary.overall:
Damien Chazelle wanted to make a film about the magic of movies. He made it by putting that magic through a meat grinder for three hours and nine minutes to see if anything noble survived the processing.

Babylon is a spectacular, exhausting, infuriating, genuinely moving piece of cinema that opens with an elephant defecating on a man's head and closes with Manny Torres weeping alone in a 1952 movie theater while Singin' in the Rain plays on screen. The distance between those two images is not ironic. It is Chazelle's entire argument: Hollywood is a machine of extraordinary vulgarity in the service of something that approaches the sacred, and the people destroyed in the making of it are part of the cost.

The film is set during Hollywood's transition from silent films to sound, roughly 1926 to 1932. This is historically the period of the Hays Code: the industry voluntarily imposing moral censorship on itself after years of increasingly scandalous content and off-screen behavior. Chazelle sets his film in the years before that reckoning, when Hollywood was genuinely Babylon: a city of limitless money, zero moral framework, and a concentrated density of human ambition that burned through people the way the era burned through film stock.

He follows five characters through this transition:

Manny Torres (Diego Calva), a Mexican immigrant who starts handling logistics at parties and ends up as a studio executive through talent, hard work, and a love for cinema that never dims.

Nellie LaRoy (Margot Robbie), a self-declared star from New Jersey who has genuine talent but no capacity for self-preservation, whose addiction to excess and chaos consumes everything she builds.

Jack Conrad (Brad Pitt), a silent film star of genuine stature whose voice and persona do not translate to sound films, who watches his career dissolve with the grace of a man who understands what he was and refuses to be less.

Sidney Palmer (Jovan Adepo), an African-American jazz trumpeter whose talent earns him entry to Hollywood but whose integrity costs him a place in it.

Lady Fay Zhu (Li Jun Li), a Chinese-American gay cabaret singer who thrives in Babylon's chaos and is then quietly discarded when the studios clean house.

Plot Summary: Rise, Excess, and the Bill That Comes Due

The film opens in 1926 at a party that must be seen to be described. It is the defining party of the silent era: unlimited cocaine, open sex, jazz, nudity, and an elephant being transported through the proceedings for reasons the film never feels the need to explain. This is where Manny, Nellie, Sidney, and Fay all exist simultaneously, in proximity to Jack Conrad. A young actress overdoses. Manny quietly manages the situation. Nellie dances until she is noticed. An era is introduced.

From there the film tracks each character's arc through the transition period. Nellie becomes a star on raw magnetism, then finds that sound films require discipline she does not possess. Manny rises through competence and genuine love for the medium, eventually becoming a studio executive and pitching Sidney's orchestra for lead billing. Jack makes increasingly low-budget films, marries multiple times, and is eventually informed by gossip columnist Elinor St. John that his star has faded, though he will be remembered forever on film. Sidney is asked to wear blackface by studio executives for a Southern market film and walks out of the industry. Fay is fired from Kinoscope when her lesbianism becomes a liability. The Hays Code tightens. The party ends.

The film's second-half turns brutal. Nellie, destroyed by addiction and debt, borrows money from gangster James McKay, loses it gambling, and ends up in a chase through underground Los Angeles involving counterfeit money, literal snakebite, and a sadistic underground party that the film depicts in genuinely disturbing detail. She vanishes from the story. Manny finds her years later, alone and broken, and she says goodbye.

Jack Conrad commits suicide. Manny leaves Los Angeles.

Years later, Manny returns to a cinema playing Singin' in the Rain (1952). He watches it in isolation: a film that romanticizes the exact era he lived through, scrubbed clean of the Babylon he knew, immortalizing the people he knew, making beautiful what was ugly. He weeps. The film then cuts through a century of cinema in a montage sequence that is either Chazelle's most ambitious moment or his most self-indulgent, depending on your tolerance.

The argument is: all of this carnage, all these destroyed lives, this river of debauchery and exploitation and racism and addiction, produced something that endures. Cinema remains. The people it burned through do not.

A note on scoring the hedonism trope: we rate it as Moderate authenticity because the film does not straightforwardly endorse what it depicts. The opening party and Nellie's arc are presented as spectacle, but Nellie is destroyed by it. The question is whether the film's aestheticization of excess functions as endorsement or warning. We score it as Moderate rather than Low because the film does aestheticize this material lavishly enough that the warning is not unambiguous, particularly in the first act.

Woke Trap Assessment

Babylon is not a woke trap. Its content is visible from the opening sequence. Conservative families who attend expecting the elegance of La La Land will discover the true nature of this film within the first fifteen minutes. Nothing is hidden. The progressive character elements, Sidney's racism storyline, Fay's lesbianism, are present and consistent throughout. The film's traditional values score comes from structural consequences, not masked ideology.

Creative Team at a Glance

Damien Chazelle is, by ideological profile, the least political major filmmaker of his generation. His films are obsessively about craft, ambition, and the price of excellence. Whiplash (2014) asked whether artistic excellence justifies cruelty. La La Land (2016) asked whether romantic love and artistic ambition can coexist. First Man (2018) asked what kind of man walks on the moon. Babylon asks what it costs to make something that outlives you.

His political statements are minimal and his film decisions track artistic ambition rather than ideology. Babylon is his only film that engages directly with race, and it does so through the lens of documented historical practice (blackface being demanded of Black performers for Southern markets was a real industry practice) rather than contemporary identity politics.

Justin Hurwitz, whose score is this film's most undeniable achievement, is a non-political collaborator whose craft anchors every Chazelle film. His Babylon score is the best argument for the film's greatness: propulsive, anachronistic, ecstatic, and finally heartbreaking.

Adult Viewer Insight: The Case For and Against Babylon

The case for Babylon is Margot Robbie, Brad Pitt at his most vulnerable, Diego Calva at his most disciplined, Justin Hurwitz's extraordinary score, and one of the most honest arguments about the relationship between art and destruction that mainstream Hollywood has made in decades. The wages-of-sin structure is real and consistent: every character who loses themselves in the excess of the era is consumed by it. Jack Conrad survives longer than most because he retains his dignity, but he too is ultimately discarded. The film argues, without ambiguity, that the Babylon of 1920s Hollywood was not a paradise but a machine that converted human lives into entertainment, and that the entertainment that survived is genuinely worth something despite the cost.

The case against Babylon is three hours and nine minutes. Chazelle loses control of his material repeatedly. The underground sadism party sequence, which involves a gangster dragging Manny and a drug dealer through a series of depravity tableaux for extended minutes, does not advance the story and exists apparently because Chazelle wanted to establish how far beneath the glamour Hollywood's underground ran. He is not wrong about this historically, but the sequence is unpleasant in a way that serves shock more than argument. The film's final montage, which cuts through cinema history to land on the implication that all movies are spiritually connected to the Babylon that made them, is either Chazelle's most ambitious gesture or a case of a director who has been making films about movies for so long that he has lost perspective on what movies are for.

For conservative viewers: Babylon is not the enemy. It is not a progressive polemic or an ideological film. It is a large, complicated, morally serious piece of filmmaking that contains content many conservative families will find deeply offensive and should not watch. The viewers who will value it most are adults with high tolerance for graphic content and genuine interest in what the film is actually arguing, which is that excess destroys, craft endures, and the cost of art is paid in people.

Verdict: TRADITIONAL LEAN. The wages-of-sin structure is present and consistent, and the film's best moments argue for the enduring value of craft, devotion, and dignified failure over dissolution. The graphic content is not endorsed but aestheticized, which is a meaningful distinction. Adults who engage with this film critically will find more traditional value in it than its reputation suggests.
summary.adultInsight: Babylon is Damien Chazelle's most ambitious and least controlled film. At 189 minutes it chronicles five characters through Hollywood's silent-to-sound transition, built around a wages-of-sin structure: every character who fully surrenders to the era's debauchery is destroyed, while the film's moral center, Mexican immigrant Manny Torres, survives through work, loyalty, and love for cinema itself. The hedonism is aestheticized but not endorsed. Margot Robbie's Nellie LaRoy is a career-best performance. Brad Pitt's Jack Conrad is quietly extraordinary. Justin Hurwitz's score may be the best of the decade so far. The film contains genuinely disturbing content (an underground sadism party sequence, graphic drug use, explicit sexuality throughout) that earns its R rating repeatedly. It is not a progressive polemic. The blackface and lesbianism subplots are historically grounded rather than ideologically weaponized. The film's thesis is pre-moral: Hollywood was Babylon, it destroyed people, and what it built has outlasted everyone it destroyed. Conservative viewers who can tolerate the content will find a film that takes seriously the question of what excellence costs and whether the cost is worth paying.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R. For adults only. The opening party sequence alone is disqualifying for anyone under 18: graphic sex, nudity, cocaine, and a scene involving bodily fluids that is neither brief nor implied. The film maintains this intensity throughout its 189-minute runtime at irregular intervals. Drug addiction is shown with consequences but also glamorized in its early stages. An underground sequence depicting animal cruelty and sadism is genuinely disturbing. Strong language throughout. LGBT content is present and not incidental. This is a serious film for serious adult viewers with high tolerance for graphic content. It is not appropriate for families or younger viewers under any circumstances.

tropeAudit.name: Aestheticized Hedonism
tropeAudit.description: The film opens with twenty minutes of the most graphically depicted debauchery in a major studio release in years. The party is filmed with genuine visual artistry: Chazelle and cinematographer Linus Sandgren shoot the chaos as spectacle, not horror. The authenticity is scored Moderate because the film's consequences do discipline the excess: every character who surrenders to it is destroyed. But the aestheticization is real and sustained enough to resist a Low authenticity score. Chazelle is not endorsing the party, but he is making it beautiful.

tropeAudit.name: Racial Discrimination / Historical Injustice
tropeAudit.description: Sidney Palmer's arc centers on the documented historical practice of studios requiring light-skinned Black performers to darken their complexions for Southern market films. Fay Zhu is fired because her lesbianism threatens studio relationships. Both subplots are historically grounded in real industry practice rather than invented for contemporary political relevance, which raises their authenticity score. The film handles both with relative restraint, letting the events speak without editorial lecturing.

tropeAudit.name: LGBT Representation
tropeAudit.description: Lady Fay Zhu is an openly gay character from her first appearance. She and Nellie share a passionate kiss. Fay's sexual identity is treated matter-of-factly by the film rather than as a special event, which mirrors the documented history of Hollywood's pre-Hays Code period when such relationships existed with relative openness before the censors arrived. The historical framing is authentic. The representation is present and not incidental.

tropeAudit.name: Moral Relativism / Consequence-Free Decline
tropeAudit.description: While the wages-of-sin structure does operate in Babylon, the film does not offer clear moral framing for why the characters who fall, fall. Nellie's destruction is presented as tragedy without moral verdict. Jack's suicide is elegiac rather than cautionary. The film mourns its characters without judging them, which is in tension with a straightforward traditional values reading. We score moral relativism as Moderate authenticity because the consequences are real even if the moral accounting is soft.

tropeAudit.name: Wages of Sin / Excess Destroys
tropeAudit.description: This is the film's structural spine. Every character who fully surrenders to the excess of 1920s Hollywood is consumed by it. Nellie LaRoy, whose talent was real and whose potential was genuine, dies alone after years of addiction and self-destruction. The underground sadism sequence makes explicit what the excess ultimately leads to: a descent through layers of depravity to something irredeemably dark. The Hays Code arrival is presented not as puritanical censorship but as an industry reckoning with what it had become. Authenticity scored Moderate because the film aestheticizes the destruction as much as it condemns it.

tropeAudit.name: Loyal Devotion Despite Desertion
tropeAudit.description: Manny Torres's sustained love and loyalty for Nellie LaRoy across years of her self-destruction and his own advancement is the film's most straightforwardly traditional element. He helps her when she has given him every reason not to. He finds her years after Hollywood has forgotten her and says a final goodbye. This is devotion without expectation of return, a classical virtue operating consistently in a morally chaotic environment.

tropeAudit.name: Art Endures / The Immortality of Craft
tropeAudit.description: Elinor St. John tells Jack Conrad that his star is fading but he will be immortalized on film. The closing sequence of Manny watching Singin' in the Rain confirms this: the people destroyed by Hollywood's machine are preserved in what that machine made. The film presents art as a legitimate transcendent value, something that outlasts the lives consumed in its making. This is a traditional argument about the relationship between craft, sacrifice, and permanence.

tropeAudit.name: American Immigrant Work Ethic
tropeAudit.description: Manny Torres is explicitly the son of impoverished Mexican refugees who rises through talent, competence, and willingness to work. His arc is a legitimate American Dream narrative: starting as an elephant handler at a party and ending as a studio executive through earned advancement rather than connection or luck. The film does not undercut this with irony. Manny's success is presented as deserved.

tropeAudit.name: Dignity in Obsolescence
tropeAudit.description: Jack Conrad faces the loss of his career with more grace than most men in a similar position. He does not rage, does not descend into bitterness, does not blame others. He marries too many times and drinks too much, but his fundamental decency persists. His suicide is a failure, but it is the failure of a man who could not adapt, not a man who chose dissolution. The film treats his decline as tragedy rather than as evidence of moral deficiency.

tropeAudit.name: Craft as Moral Anchor
tropeAudit.description: The characters who retain their integrity longest are those who remain committed to their craft: Manny's dedication to making good films even as the industry deteriorates, Jack's professionalism even in B-pictures, Sidney's refusal to compromise his musical integrity for the Southern market. The film consistently presents craft commitment as a form of moral seriousness even in an environment without explicit moral structure.

title: The Menu
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Margin is positive (barely). Not a woke trap. The film's class warfare satire is front and center within the first fifteen minutes. There is no bait-and-switch. Conservative viewers will know exactly what they are dealing with well before the halfway point.

director.name: Mark Mylod
director.ideology: CENTER-LEFT. Primarily a television director known for Succession and Game of Thrones. His sensibility is satirical, dark, and class-conscious without being overtly political. He does not moralize; he observes and then burns things down.
director.profile: British director Mark Mylod built his reputation directing prestige television, most notably Succession (multiple Emmy awards) and Game of Thrones. The Menu is his most prominent theatrical feature. His background in Succession is evident throughout: the same razor-sharp class observation, the same black humor about wealthy people trapped in systems of their own making, the same preference for letting characters damn themselves rather than delivering moral lectures. Mylod is a craftsman first and an ideologue never. His instincts align more with social satire than political messaging. The film's visual control, tight 107-minute runtime, and willingness to withhold easy resolution all reflect his television background elevated to theatrical ambition.

writers.profile: Seth Reiss and Will Tracy met writing for The Onion and Late Night with Seth Meyers. Tracy also wrote White Noise (2022) for Noah Baumbach. Their background in satirical comedy shapes the film's tone: it is designed to be funny and unsettling simultaneously, never earnest about its class critique. The script is disciplined in a way that pure ideology rarely is. It finds its themes through character logic rather than statement. Margot's eventual escape via the cheeseburger is not a political lesson; it is a character beat that happens to carry meaning. That distinction matters.

lead_producer.name: Adam McKay, Betsy Koch, Will Ferrell
lead_producer.company: Hyperobject Industries / Gary Sanchez Productions / Searchlight Pictures

composer.name: Colin Stetson
composer.profile: Experimental musician and composer known for intense, unnerving work. His score for The Menu relies on discordant tones and deliberate tension-building. It refuses to comfort the audience when they want it.

top_cast.name: Ralph Fiennes
top_cast.notes: The film is built around Fiennes' performance and it earns every second of his screen time. Slowik is frightening not because he is manic but because he is completely calm. He has made peace with his own darkness. Fiennes plays him with a stillness that is more disturbing than any amount of screaming could be. His earlier ease and later collapse into nihilism are both utterly convincing. Golden Globe nominated.

top_cast.name: Anya Taylor-Joy
top_cast.notes: The moral center of the film and its only character with real survival instinct. Taylor-Joy plays Margot as perceptive and pragmatic: she is the only guest who sees Slowik clearly because she is the only one without something to prove. Her cheeseburger scene is the film's best moment, and she plays it with perfect low-key wit.

top_cast.name: Nicholas Hoult
top_cast.notes: Plays the film's most contemptible character: a food obsessive so invested in the mythology of Chef Slowik that he knowingly escorts a woman to her death for the experience. Hoult makes Tyler pathetic rather than monstrous, which is the harder and more interesting choice. His kitchen humiliation scene is brutal.

top_cast.name: Janet McTeer
top_cast.notes: The film reserves special venom for the critical class, and McTeer's performance earns it. Lillian is the kind of powerful critic who has turned her personal taste into institutional authority. She is fascinating and awful in equal measure.

fidelityCasting.assessment: The Menu is an original production with no source adaptation to evaluate. The casting is largely accurate to the script's intentions. Anya Taylor-Joy was cast specifically because her unconventional look reinforced Margot's status as someone who does not belong in this world. Ralph Fiennes embodies the creative-genius-turned-nihilist archetype without relying on obvious menace cues.

A character shoots himself in the head (shown)

parentalGuidance.parentalNotes: This is a hard R film intended for adults. The violence is precise and shocking rather than gratuitous, but it is genuinely disturbing. Not appropriate for children or younger teens. Conservative families should be aware that the film contains a sympathetic escort character and depicts sexual harassment explicitly. The satire targets elites across the political spectrum.

summary.overall:
The Menu is a slick, well-crafted class satire that will make you laugh and make you uneasy, sometimes at the same time. It is also a film whose ideological message is more muddled than its admirers want to admit.

The setup is elegant. A group of wealthy diners travel to a remote island restaurant run by celebrity chef Julian Slowik (Ralph Fiennes, terrifying and still). Over the course of the evening, Slowik reveals that the menu has a purpose beyond food: each guest is there to be punished for what they represent. The film makes them all complicit in something. The food critic who destroyed careers with her reviews. The wealthy regulars who treated the restaurant as a symbol of their status. The tech bros who exploit other people's work. The faded movie star coasting on name recognition. And Tyler, the food obsessive who brought his date knowing she would die, because the experience was worth more to him than she was.

Only Margot (Anya Taylor-Joy) escapes, and the reason she escapes is the film's thesis statement. She orders a cheeseburger. Not because she is clever about it but because she is hungry and the food she has been served is, in her direct assessment, 'loveless.' Slowik finds joy in making it. A real thing, made with real care, for a real person. The pretension falls away. The artifice collapses. The cheeseburger saves her life.

There is something genuinely conservative in that message, and I mean that as a compliment. The film has contempt for the people who have elevated food (and by extension, art, culture, entertainment) into a status competition so abstract it has lost all connection to the thing itself. The food critic destroys chefs for sport. The foodie Tyler cannot taste anymore; he can only evaluate. The wealthy diners do not eat; they perform. The film is savagely funny about all of this, and its contempt feels earned rather than cheap.

But. The film also frames Slowik's rampage as a kind of labor uprising. He had his passion destroyed by the consumer class. His staff follow him into death with cultish devotion because he is the only person who ever saw them as skilled workers rather than service employees. The anti-capitalist reading is available, and the film does not work hard to prevent you from taking it.

This is what pushes the score to MIXED rather than TRADITIONAL LEAN. The film critiques both the consumer class and the artist class. It celebrates authenticity over pretension. But it also positions the service and creative worker as exploited victims of a rigged economic system. Both critiques are present and neither one fully wins.

Ralph Fiennes is extraordinary. He is genuinely frightening in a role that could easily tip into camp. Anya Taylor-Joy is the best she has been in a long time. The film is 107 minutes and does not waste a single one.

The question for conservative viewers is: can you enjoy a darkly funny film about wealthy people getting what they deserve, even if the economic framing occasionally tilts left? If the answer is yes, The Menu is one of the more sharply crafted genre films of 2022. If you need your entertainment to be ideologically tidy, look elsewhere.
summary.oneLiner: A masterfully crafted class satire where the cheeseburger is the conservative hero and the food critics deserve everything they get. Brilliant filmmaking, mixed message.
summary.verdict: The Menu's contempt for cultural pretension and status-obsessed elites plays as conservative instinct. The anti-capitalist undercurrent muddies the waters. Ralph Fiennes is one of the best performances of 2022. Worth watching.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults will find much to enjoy in The Menu's savaging of pretentious cultural elites. The film's core argument, that authenticity and directness defeat artifice every time, aligns with traditional values. The economic framing occasionally veers left. But Mylod is too sharp a director to let ideology overwhelm craft. Watch it for Fiennes and Taylor-Joy. Think about it for the cheeseburger.
summary.parentalGuidance: Hard R. Adults only. Strong violence, disturbing content, sexual references. Not appropriate for children or teens.

tropeAudit.name: Class Warfare Anti-Capitalist Satire
tropeAudit.description: The film's central engine is class resentment directed upward. Slowik punishes the consumer class, the investor class, and the celebrity class for destroying his passion for craft. His staff function as an organized labor force who follow him into collective death rather than continue serving the wealthy. The anti-capitalist reading is available and the script invites it. Producer Adam McKay (The Big Short, Don't Look Up) is a committed left-wing satirist whose fingerprints are on the film's political sensibility.

tropeAudit.name: Toxic Masculinity / Male Ego Critique
tropeAudit.description: Tyler's obsessive foodie culture and his willingness to sacrifice Margot for an experience are framed as the logical endpoint of a particular kind of male ego. Slowik's loss of passion is also partly attributed to male pride and the inability to accept limitations. Neither critique is sustained or explicit, but the film returns to male ego as a form of corruption multiple times.

tropeAudit.name: Sexual Harassment Addressed / Male Abuser Consequences
tropeAudit.description: Slowik allows himself to be stabbed by Katherine, an employee he sexually harassed. The scene is handled with minimal drama: Slowik presents his own punishment as part of the menu. The #MeToo resonance is clear but not heavy-handed. The film is not primarily about this; it is one note in a larger chord.

tropeAudit.name: Authenticity Over Pretension / Cheeseburger as Truth
tropeAudit.description: Margot escapes because she asks for something real. A cheeseburger. Not the elaborate symbolic dish Slowik has prepared to make a point, but actual food made with care for an actual hungry person. Slowik responds to it because it strips away the performance and returns to the original thing: a cook making food for someone who wants to eat it. This is a deeply traditional insight. The film's climax rewards directness, simplicity, and the refusal to participate in elite cultural performance.

tropeAudit.name: Elite Cultural Class Savaged / Critics and Elites Punished
tropeAudit.description: The film reserves its most sustained contempt for the food critic Lillian Bloom, whose entire career is framed as parasitic destruction of creative work she cannot match. The wealthy regulars are shown as status-seekers with no relationship to the actual food. The tech bros are oblivious and cruel. This is not a left-wing critique of capitalism; it is a very old critique of the corrupt cultural establishment that pretends to judge merit while serving its own interests.

tropeAudit.name: Common Sense / Working Class Pragmatism Rewarded
tropeAudit.description: Margot is not the smartest character in the film and not the bravest. She survives because she is pragmatic. She does not play the game. She does not perform sophistication she does not feel. She asks for what she actually wants and is honest about who she is when pressed. In a film full of people performing cultural sophistication, her refusal to perform is treated as the only authentic act. The film rewards working-class directness over elite pretension.

detailed_analysis:
The Menu is a film that conservative critics have largely misread. They see the anti-capitalist messaging and dismiss it. They miss the cheeseburger.

The film's thesis is actually quite old and quite traditional: authenticity defeats performance. Margot survives not because she is ideologically correct but because she is real. She does not pretend to be something she is not. She does not participate in Slowik's performance. She asks for what she actually wants.

This is why the film is MIXED rather than WOKE. Both the class critique and the authenticity-over-pretension message are present and neither fully wins. The film is content to hold both simultaneously.

For conservative viewers, the practical question is whether you can extract value from a film whose economic framing occasionally tilts left. The answer should be yes. The Menu's contempt for the critical class, for cultural status performance, and for the parasitic relationship between wealthy consumers and working artists is sharp and funny and earned. Ralph Fiennes gives one of the great villain performances of the decade.

comparison_films.reason: Same director, same class satire sensibility, same willingness to make everyone complicit

comparison_films.title: Knives Out (2019)
comparison_films.reason: Similarly structured class satire with a working-class protagonist who sees through elite performance
